title: Data Visualisation with Matplotlib, Seaborn and Plotly
subtitle: Choose the right chart, build it precisely with Matplotlib, explore data with seaborn, share interactive charts with Plotly, and make every figure clear, accessible and ready to publish.
outcomes: Choose a chart from the question and the data, and know when a table or a single number works better
Build and fine-tune multi-panel figures with Matplotlib's figure and axes interface: ticks, formatters, styles and layouts
Explore distributions, relationships and categories with seaborn's statistical plots and facets
Make interactive Plotly Express charts with hover details, facets and animation, and share them as HTML
Use colour purposefully and accessibly, annotate what matters, and export figures at the right size and format
prerequisites: Python and basic pandas: loading a CSV, selecting columns and grouping (Data Analysis with Python and pandas covers them, with a first look at Matplotlib). You need Python 3.11 or later; the course installs Matplotlib, seaborn, Plotly and pandas in a virtual environment, and the data comes with the labs. Google Chrome is used once, to simulate colour vision deficiency.
description:
A good chart answers a question at a glance; a poor one hides the answer or suggests the wrong one. This course teaches you to make the good kind with Python's three most widely used plotting libraries, using two years of (made-up) surveys from six coral reef sites and the fish measured there. You'll start by choosing charts from the question being asked, then learn Matplotlib's figure and axes model properly: multi-panel figures, ticks and formatters, dates, styles and layouts. Seaborn then turns tidy data into statistical plots in a line each: histograms, density curves and ECDFs, box and violin plots, confidence intervals and heatmaps.

Next you'll build interactive charts with Plotly Express, with hover labels, facets and animation, and publish them as web pages. The last two modules are about design: colour that fits the data, figures that work for readers with colour vision deficiency (you'll check contrast with the WCAG formula and simulate how others see your charts), annotation that points out what matters, small multiples instead of spaghetti charts, and exporting at the right size and format for screens, slides and print. Every module has a lab whose scripts print exact results to check, and the capstone is a visual report on reef health, rebuilt from the data by one script. It builds on Data Analysis with Python and pandas and leads on to Data Storytelling and Dashboard Design and Interactive Data Apps with Streamlit.

modules.title: Choosing charts and Matplotlib's figure model
modules.summary: Match the chart to the question and the data, then build figures precisely with Matplotlib's object-oriented interface: figures, axes, ticks, formatters and styles.

lessons.title: Choosing a chart for the question
objectives: Match common analytical questions to the chart types that answer them
Explain why position and length are read more accurately than angle, area or colour
Recognise when a table or a single number works better than a chart
key_points: Start from the question: comparing amounts across categories suits bars or a dot plot, change over time suits a line, a distribution suits a histogram, box plot or violin, a relationship between two numbers suits a scatter plot, and parts of a whole suit a stacked or 100% bar.

Readers judge position along a shared scale most accurately, then length, then angle and area, with colour shade the least precise, as Cleveland and McGill's graphical perception experiments (1984) showed; so put the comparison that matters on a common axis.

Bars encode values by their length, so a bar chart's value axis must start at zero; a dot plot encodes them by position, so its axis can start elsewhere, which makes it the better choice for close values such as temperatures.

Part-to-whole charts get hard to read beyond a few parts: a pie with more than about five slices, or a stacked bar whose middle segments float, hides the comparisons; side-by-side bars usually show them better.

When readers need exact values or will look things up, use a table; when one number matters most, show the number itself, large, with its comparison, such as 'coral cover 34%, down 6 points on last year'.

lessons.title: Figures, axes and the object-oriented interface
objectives: Describe the parts of a Matplotlib figure: Figure, Axes, Axis and Artists
Create figures with plt.subplots and draw with Axes methods instead of pyplot's current-axes functions
Save figures from a script with a non-interactive backend
key_points: A Figure is the whole image; it holds one or more Axes, each a single plot with its own x and y Axis objects, and everything drawn, from lines and bars to text, is an Artist belonging to an Axes or to the Figure.
fig, ax = plt.subplots() gives one Axes; plt.subplots(2, 2) returns a 2-by-2 NumPy array of Axes, so axs[0, 1] is the top-right panel and axs.flat runs through all of them in reading order.

Matplotlib has two interfaces: pyplot functions such as plt.plot act on the 'current' Axes, which is quick for one chart but confusing with several, while the object-oriented style calls methods on named objects, such as ax.plot and ax.set_title, and stays clear in scripts and functions.

Most pyplot functions have an Axes method with a set_ prefix: plt.title becomes ax.set_title, plt.xlabel becomes ax.set_xlabel and plt.xlim becomes ax.set_xlim; ax.set(title=..., xlabel=...) sets several at once.
layout='constrained' in plt.subplots makes room for titles, labels and legends so panels don't overlap, and is more flexible than calling fig.tight_layout() at the end.
In a script that only saves files, matplotlib.use('Agg') selects a non-interactive backend, so nothing tries to open a window; fig.savefig writes the file and plt.close(fig) frees its memory.

lessons.title: Ticks, labels, formatters and styles
objectives: Set limits and ticks, and format tick labels as percentages, thousands or dates
Remove clutter such as the top and right spines
Apply a style sheet or rcParams so every figure in a project looks consistent
key_points: ax.set_xlim and ax.set_ylim fix the visible range, ax.set_xticks chooses where the ticks go (labels= sets their text) and ax.tick_params changes their size, direction and colour.

Formatters in matplotlib.ticker turn tick values into readable text: PercentFormatter(100) shows 40 as 40%, and ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter('{x:,.0f}') adds thousands separators; any function of the value and position also works as a formatter.
Plot dates as datetime values, not strings, which Matplotlib treats as categories; matplotlib.dates.ConciseDateFormatter then labels the ticks compactly, showing the year once where it changes.
ax.spines[['top', 'right']].set_visible(False) removes the top and right lines of the box, and light gridlines from ax.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3) help readers read values without dominating the chart.

plt.style.use('seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid'), or any name in plt.style.available, styles every later figure; with plt.style.context(...) applies a style inside a with block only, and plt.rcParams['font.size'] = 11 changes one default.
A project style sheet, a text file such as report.mplstyle with lines like axes.spines.top: False, keeps every figure consistent: load it with plt.style.use('report.mplstyle').

"""Reef overview: four panels drawn with Matplotlib's object-oriented interface."""
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")                     # save to files; no window needed
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter

df = pd.read_csv("reef_surveys.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
print(f"{len(df)} surveys at {df['site'].nunique()} sites, {df['date'].min():%b %Y} to {df['date'].max():%b %Y}")

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 7), layout="constrained")
ax_temp, ax_cover, ax_hist, ax_scatter = axs.flat

# Panel 1: change over time, so a line for each zone
temp = df.groupby(["date", "zone"])["water_temp_c"].mean().unstack()
for zone in temp.columns:
    ax_temp.plot(temp.index, temp[zone], label=zone)
ax_temp.set_title("Water temperature by zone")
ax_temp.set_ylabel("Mean temperature (°C)")
ax_temp.legend(frameon=False)
locator = mdates.AutoDateLocator()
ax_temp.xaxis.set_major_locator(locator)
ax_temp.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.ConciseDateFormatter(locator))

hints: If the first panel's dates are squashed or missing, check that read_csv has parse_dates=['date']: dates read as text become categories.
The pixel size is figsize times dpi only without bbox_inches='tight', which trims the margins, so this lab leaves it out.

If panels overlap, check that plt.subplots has layout='constrained' (Matplotlib 3.6 or later).

modules.title: Statistical plots with seaborn
modules.summary: Use seaborn's dataset-oriented functions, built on Matplotlib, to show distributions, compare groups, plot relationships with their uncertainty and draw annotated heatmaps.

lessons.title: How seaborn works: long data, mappings and figure-level functions
objectives: Explain why seaborn wants long (tidy) data and how x, y, hue, size and style map columns to what you see
Choose between axes-level and figure-level functions
Set a theme, and combine seaborn with Matplotlib through ax=
key_points: Seaborn plots a DataFrame by column name: sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='water_temp_c', y='bleached_pct', hue='zone') colours the points by zone and adds a legend, with no loop.

It works best with long (tidy) data, one row per observation and one column per variable; a wide table with one column per site can be reshaped with df.melt(id_vars='date', var_name='site', value_name='cover').

Axes-level functions such as histplot, boxplot and scatterplot draw on one Matplotlib Axes and take ax=, so they fit into your own subplots; figure-level functions (relplot, displot and catplot) create their own figure and can split it into facets with col= and row=.

A figure-level function returns a FacetGrid: size it with height= and aspect= rather than figsize, label it with g.set_axis_labels and g.set_titles, reach its Matplotlib Figure as g.figure and save it with g.savefig.
sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid', context='notebook') sets the look of every later plot; the contexts paper, notebook, talk and poster scale fonts and lines for where the figure will be seen.

lessons.title: Distributions: histograms, density and box plots
objectives: Show a distribution with a histogram, KDE or ECDF, choosing bins or bandwidth deliberately
Compare distributions across groups with box, violin and strip plots
key_points: sns.histplot counts values in bins, and binwidth= or bins= changes the picture, so try more than one; stat='percent' or 'density' makes groups of different sizes comparable, and common_norm=False normalises each hue group on its own.

A kernel density estimate (sns.kdeplot, or kde=True in histplot) is a smoothed histogram: bw_adjust below 1 shows more detail and above 1 smooths more, and the curve can run past the data's real limits, such as below zero, which cut=0 prevents.

An ECDF (sns.ecdfplot) shows, for every value, the proportion of observations at or below it: there are no bins or smoothing to choose, and medians and other percentiles can be read straight off the y-axis.

A box plot shows the median, the quartiles (the box holds the middle 50%) and whiskers reaching the furthest points within 1.5 times the IQR (the length of the box), with points beyond drawn singly; a violin plot shows the shape of a KDE instead.
Box plots hide sample size and shape, such as two peaks, so for small groups add the points with sns.stripplot (or swarmplot, which avoids overlaps) and say how many observations each group has.

lessons.title: Relationships, categories and heatmaps
objectives: Plot relationships with scatterplot, lineplot and regplot, and read their confidence bands
Compare categories with barplot, pointplot and countplot, knowing what their bars and error bars show
Draw an annotated heatmap of a pivot table or a correlation matrix
key_points: sns.lineplot aggregates repeated x values: it draws the mean at each x with a shaded 95% confidence interval by default; errorbar='sd' shows the standard deviation instead and errorbar=None removes the band.

sns.barplot shows a summary, the mean by default (estimator= changes it), with an error bar, not the number of rows; sns.countplot shows how many rows each category has, and sns.pointplot shows the same means as points joined by lines.
sns.regplot and sns.lmplot add a least-squares regression line with a confidence band; the line describes a trend in this sample, can miss a threshold or a curve, and is not evidence of cause.

sns.heatmap colours a grid of numbers, such as df.pivot_table(index='site', columns='family', values='length_cm'); annot=True writes each value in its cell, fmt='.1f' formats it and cmap= chooses the palette.

A correlation matrix runs from -1 to 1, so give it a diverging palette centred on zero, as in sns.heatmap(corr, vmin=-1, vmax=1, center=0, cmap='vlag'), so that a colour means the same thing in every chart.

lab.title: Explore fish lengths with seaborn
lab.goal: Describe 240 fish measured on the reef transects with seaborn's statistical plots: each family's distribution, how the two zones compare, what a bar of means hides and where the longest fish are.
setup: The virtual environment from the module 1 lab, with seaborn installed
The starter files fish_plots.py and fish_lengths.csv (240 made-up fish from four families, 60 of each and half from each zone), in your course folder; the capstone uses the CSV again

steps.do: Put the two files in your course folder and run the starter. It sets a theme, loads the fish and orders the families by median length, an order every plot will reuse.
steps.code: python fish_plots.py
steps.see: 240 fish measured. Families, shortest median first: Butterflyfish, Surgeonfish, Parrotfish, Grouper

steps.do: Add one histogram per family with a KDE curve, using the figure-level displot to make the facets.
steps.code:
# 1. One histogram per family, with a KDE curve: a figure-level function makes the facets
g = sns.displot(fish, x="length_cm", col="family", col_order=order, col_wrap=2,
                binwidth=2, kde=True, height=2.6, aspect=1.4)
g.set_axis_labels("Length (cm)", "Fish")
g.set_titles("{col_name}")
g.savefig("fish_length_histograms.png", dpi=120)
print("Saved fish_length_histograms.png with", len(g.axes.flat), "panels")
steps.see: Saved fish_length_histograms.png with 4 panels

steps.do: Compare the zones within each family with split violins that mark the quartiles, and print the difference in median length.
steps.code:
# 2. Compare the two zones within each family: split violins with the quartiles marked
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5), layout="constrained")
sns.violinplot(fish, x="family", y="length_cm", hue="zone", order=order, split=True, inner="quart", cut=0, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Length (cm)", title="Outer-reef fish are a little longer in most families")
fig.savefig("fish_length_by_zone.png", dpi=120)
plt.close(fig)
medians = fish.pivot_table(index="family", columns="zone", values="length_cm", aggfunc="median").loc[order]
print((medians["outer reef"] - medians["lagoon"]).round(1).rename("outer minus lagoon, cm").to_string())
steps.see: Butterflyfish 2.9, Surgeonfish 2.4, Parrotfish 2.4 and Grouper 2.8 cm longer on the outer reef.

steps.do: Draw ECDFs, with a reference line at 30 cm, and print the share of each family that is longer.
steps.code:
# 3. ECDFs: the share of fish at or below each length, with no bins to choose
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4), layout="constrained")
sns.ecdfplot(fish, x="length_cm", hue="family", hue_order=order, ax=ax)
ax.axvline(30, color="grey", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.set(xlabel="Length (cm)", ylabel="Proportion of fish at or below")
fig.savefig("fish_length_ecdf.png", dpi=120)
plt.close(fig)
share = (fish["length_cm"] > 30).groupby(fish["family"]).mean().loc[order]
print("Longer than 30 cm:", ", ".join(f"{family} {s:.0%}" for family, s in share.items()))
steps.see: Longer than 30 cm: Butterflyfish 0%, Surgeonfish 3%, Parrotfish 45%, Grouper 82%

steps.do: Put a bar chart of means with 95% confidence intervals next to a count plot of how many fish each bar is based on. seed=1 makes the bootstrapped intervals repeatable.
steps.code:
# 4. Mean length with a 95% confidence interval, next to the raw counts
fig, (ax_mean, ax_count) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), layout="constrained")
sns.barplot(fish, x="family", y="length_cm", order=order, errorbar=("ci", 95), seed=1, ax=ax_mean)
ax_mean.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Mean length (cm)", title="Mean and 95% CI")
sns.countplot(fish, x="family", hue="zone", order=order, ax=ax_count)
ax_count.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Fish measured", title="How many fish each bar is based on")
fig.savefig("fish_mean_and_counts.png", dpi=120)
plt.close(fig)
print("Fish per family and zone:", fish.groupby(["family", "zone"]).size().unique().tolist())
steps.see: Fish per family and zone: [30]

steps.do: Finish with an annotated heatmap of median length by site and family.
steps.code:
# 5. A heatmap of median length by site and family
grid = fish.pivot_table(index="site", columns="family", values="length_cm", aggfunc="median")[order]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4), layout="constrained")
sns.heatmap(grid, annot=True, fmt=".1f", cmap="crest", cbar_kws={"label": "Median length (cm)"}, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="", title="Median fish length by site")
fig.savefig("length_heatmap.png", dpi=120)
plt.close(fig)
print("Longest median grouper:", grid["Grouper"].idxmax(), grid["Grouper"].max())
steps.see: Longest median grouper: East Slope 41.0

modules.title: Interactive charts with Plotly Express
modules.summary: Build interactive charts in one call with Plotly Express, add hover details, facets and animation, refine them through the figure object and share them as HTML pages.

lessons.title: Plotly Express: a chart from a DataFrame in one call
objectives: Create scatter, line, bar and histogram charts with Plotly Express
Control hover labels, axis labels and templates
Explain how a Plotly figure is made of data (traces) and layout
key_points: Plotly Express (import plotly.express as px) builds a whole chart from a DataFrame and column names in one call: px.scatter(df, x='water_temp_c', y='bleached_pct', color='zone') draws the points, the legend and the hover labels.
Every call returns a plotly.graph_objects Figure: fig.show() displays it in a notebook or a browser tab, and fig.write_html('chart.html') saves it as a page anyone can open.

hover_name= puts a column in bold at the top of each hover label, hover_data= adds columns (or hides one, with False), and labels={'water_temp_c': 'Water temperature (°C)'} renames a column everywhere it appears, from the axes to the legend.
A figure is data plus layout: fig.data is a tuple of traces, one per colour group in Plotly Express, and fig.layout holds the title, axes, legend and template; print(fig) shows both.
template='plotly_white' or 'simple_white' replaces the default grey background, and plotly.io's templates.default = 'plotly_white' sets it for every chart that follows.

lessons.title: Facets, animation and refining a figure
objectives: Split a chart into facets and animate it over time
Refine a figure with update_layout, update_traces and update_xaxes
Add traces, lines and shaded periods when Plotly Express alone isn't enough
key_points: facet_col= and facet_row= make small multiples that share their axes, and facet_col_wrap= wraps them into rows; facet titles read 'zone=lagoon', which fig.for_each_annotation(lambda a: a.update(text=a.text.split('=')[-1])) shortens.
animation_frame='month' adds a play button and a slider with one frame per value; animation_group= follows the same object from frame to frame, and fixed range_x= and range_y= stop the axes jumping.

fig.update_layout changes figure-wide settings (title, legend, margins, hovermode='x unified'), fig.update_traces changes every trace (marker size, line width) and fig.update_xaxes or update_yaxes changes axes, such as ticksuffix='%'.

Interaction comes built in: hover for values, drag to zoom, double-click to zoom back out, click a legend item to hide its trace and double-click one to show it alone; the toolbar's camera button downloads the current view as a PNG.

plotly.graph_objects builds traces by hand (go.Scatter, go.Bar) when a chart needs more control, and fig.add_trace, fig.add_hline and fig.add_vrect add series, threshold lines and shaded periods to a Plotly Express figure.

lessons.title: Sharing interactive charts, and when to stay static
objectives: Save interactive charts as HTML and choose how plotly.js is included
Export static images when they're needed
Decide when interactivity helps a reader and when a static figure is better
key_points: fig.write_html('chart.html') embeds the plotly.js library, several megabytes, so the file works offline; include_plotlyjs='cdn' links to the library online instead, giving a file of a few kilobytes that needs an internet connection to display.
Several charts can share one page: fig.to_html(full_html=False) returns just a chart's part of the page, and including plotly.js with the first chart only loads the library once.

Static images, with fig.write_image('chart.png'), need the separate kaleido package, and recent kaleido versions also need a Chrome or Chromium browser on the machine; Plotly's plotly_get_chrome command installs one.

Interactivity suits exploration and dashboards, where readers ask their own questions; for a report, a slide or print, a static chart with the key values labelled is clearer, because nobody can hover over paper.
Hover labels don't replace labels: put the message and the important values in the visible chart, and keep hover for detail that only some readers will want.

modules.title: Colour, accessibility and annotation
modules.summary: Choose palettes that fit the data, design figures that still work for readers with colour vision deficiency, and annotate charts so the important point can't be missed.

lessons.title: Choosing colour with a purpose
objectives: Choose qualitative, sequential or diverging palettes to match the data
Explain why perceptually uniform colormaps such as viridis beat rainbow maps
Use grey and a single accent colour to focus attention
key_points: Match the palette to the data: qualitative palettes (distinct hues, such as tab10 or seaborn's 'colorblind') for unordered categories, sequential palettes (light to dark, such as viridis or Blues) for ordered values, and diverging palettes (two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint, such as RdBu or vlag) for values either side of a meaningful centre.

Perceptually uniform colormaps such as viridis, cividis, magma and inferno change lightness evenly, so equal steps in the data look like equal steps in colour, and they still read in greyscale; rainbow maps such as jet create false boundaries where the hue changes quickly.

Centre a diverging map on the value that means 'no change', such as zero or a baseline: in Matplotlib with matplotlib.colors.TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0) or CenteredNorm(), and in seaborn's heatmap with center=.
Distinct hues get hard to tell apart beyond about six to eight categories: group the rest as 'Other', label lines directly, or use small multiples instead of more colours.

Grey plus one accent is the strongest way to direct attention: draw the context in light grey and the series that matters in one saturated colour, and keep the same colour for the same thing in every chart of a report.

lessons.title: Designing for colour vision deficiency and contrast
objectives: Choose palettes that stay distinguishable for readers with colour vision deficiency
Check the contrast of text and lines against the WCAG ratios
Write alternative text for a chart
key_points: Red-green colour vision deficiency is common, affecting roughly 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women of northern European ancestry, so never rely on red against green to mean bad and good; blue and orange, as in the Okabe-Ito palette, stay distinct for most readers.

Matplotlib's styles 'tableau-colorblind10' and 'petroff10' (petroff10 needs Matplotlib 3.10 or later) and seaborn's 'colorblind' palette are designed to stay distinguishable; check your figure anyway with a simulator, such as Chrome DevTools' vision deficiency emulation or the free Color Oracle.
Don't rely on colour alone: add a second cue such as a direct label, a marker shape or a line style (linestyle='--'), or hatching on bars, so the chart works in greyscale and for every reader.

WCAG 2 asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and for graphical objects such as lines and bars; the ratio compares the relative luminance of two colours and runs from 1:1 to 21:1.
Pale yellows, light oranges and light greys usually fail against white: keep them for backgrounds and context, and darken a colour that's too faint rather than only thickening its line.

Alternative text says what the chart is and its main point, such as 'Line chart of bleaching at six sites, 2024-2025: the lagoon sites peaked at 58% in March 2025'; offer the data as a table or a download for anyone who needs the numbers.

ax.text(0.02, 0.95, 'Source: ...', transform=ax.transAxes) places text relative to the Axes, where (0, 0) is the bottom left and (1, 1) the top right, so it stays put whatever the data limits.

Reference lines and periods give context: ax.axhline(30, linestyle='--') draws a threshold, ax.axvspan(start, end, alpha=0.15) shades a period, and ax.bar_label(bars, fmt='%.1f') prints each bar's value on it.
Direct labels, written beside each line in the line's own colour with ax.text or ax.annotate, are quicker to read than a legend that sends the eye back and forth.
In Plotly, fig.add_annotation(x=..., y=..., text=..., showarrow=True) adds a callout, and fig.add_hline and fig.add_vrect add thresholds and shaded periods, with annotation_text= for a label.
Annotate sparingly: one to three callouts that support the chart's message; when every point has a note, none of them stands out.

"""Make the bleaching chart readable for everyone: contrast, colour and annotation."""
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter


def relative_luminance(hex_colour):
    """WCAG 2 relative luminance of a colour written like '#0072B2'."""
    hex_colour = hex_colour.lstrip("#")
    channels = [int(hex_colour[i:i + 2], 16) / 255 for i in (0, 2, 4)]
    r, g, b = [c / 12.92 if c <= 0.04045 else ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4 for c in channels]
    return 0.2126 * r + 0.7152 * g + 0.0722 * b


def contrast_ratio(colour, background="#FFFFFF"):
    """WCAG contrast ratio, from 1 (no contrast) to 21 (black on white)."""
    lighter, darker = sorted([relative_luminance(colour), relative_luminance(background)], reverse=True)
    return (lighter + 0.05) / (darker + 0.05)


reef = pd.read_csv("reef_surveys.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
by_site = reef.pivot_table(index="date", columns="site", values="bleached_pct")
by_zone = reef.pivot_table(index="date", columns="zone", values="bleached_pct")
print(f"Black on white: {contrast_ratio('#000000'):.1f}:1")

hints: Contrast is about lightness, not hue: two colours of different hue but similar lightness, like orange and sky blue, can both fail against white.
If an annotation's arrow points at the wrong place, remember that xy is in data coordinates: a date on the x-axis and a percentage on the y-axis.
WCAG's 3:1 minimum for graphical objects applies to the parts needed to understand the chart; light grey context lines can be fainter, as long as the message doesn't depend on them.

modules.title: Small multiples, layout and publishing figures
modules.summary: Split crowded charts into small multiples, lay out multi-panel figures precisely, and export them at the right size, resolution and format for screens, slides and print.

lessons.title: Small multiples
objectives: Explain when small multiples beat one crowded chart
Build small multiples with shared axes in Matplotlib, seaborn and Plotly
Highlight one series against the others in each panel
key_points: Small multiples repeat the same chart for each group, such as one line chart per site, so readers compare patterns without untangling a 'spaghetti' chart of overlapping lines.
Panels must share their scales to be compared: plt.subplots(2, 3, sharex=True, sharey=True) in Matplotlib, while seaborn's figure-level functions and Plotly Express facets share axes by default.
Order the panels by something meaningful, such as zone or the size of the change, rather than alphabetically, and wrap a long row with col_wrap= in seaborn or facet_col_wrap= in Plotly.
Draw every group in light grey in each panel and the panel's own group in colour on top, so each panel shows one group against the whole.
Freeing the y-axis per panel, with fig.update_yaxes(matches=None) in Plotly or sharey=False, shows each group's shape but hides differences in size; when you do it, say so in the title or caption.

lessons.title: Laying out multi-panel figures
objectives: Lay out uneven grids of panels with subplot_mosaic or GridSpec
Size figures in inches and points for where they'll be seen
Label a whole figure once with figure-level titles
key_points: fig.subplot_mosaic('AAB;CCB') builds an uneven grid from a picture of the layout, one letter per panel and ; between rows, and returns a dictionary of Axes keyed by the letters, so axd['B'] is the tall panel on the right.
plt.subplots also takes width_ratios= and height_ratios=, and GridSpec gives finer control: gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 3) and fig.add_subplot(gs[0, :]) make a panel that spans the whole top row.
figsize is in inches and font sizes are in points (1/72 of an inch), so a 12-by-8-inch figure shrunk onto half a slide makes its 10-point labels tiny: draw the figure at the size it will be shown.

fig.suptitle, fig.supxlabel and fig.supylabel label the whole figure once instead of every panel, and with shared axes only the outer panels need tick labels (plt.subplots hides the inner ones, and ax.label_outer() does it by hand).
Subfigures, from fig.subfigures(1, 2), split a figure into blocks that each have their own panels, suptitle and layout, for a figure made of two related sets of charts.

lessons.title: Saving figures for screens, slides and print
objectives: Choose PNG, SVG or PDF for where the figure is going
Set the resolution, margins and background when saving
Export every figure reproducibly from one script
key_points: PNG is a raster format (a grid of pixels), good for screens, documents and slides; SVG and PDF are vector formats that stay sharp at any size and suit print, journals and editing in design tools; JPEG's lossy compression blurs the edges of lines and text.

dpi sets the pixels per inch of raster output: Matplotlib's default 6.4-by-4.8-inch figure saved at dpi=150 is 960 by 720 pixels; 150 to 200 dpi suits screens, print often asks for 300, and dpi doesn't change a vector file's sharpness.

bbox_inches='tight' trims empty margins, so the saved size differs from figsize, and pad_inches= sets the margin it keeps; transparent=True or facecolor= controls the background, which matters on a dark slide.
SVG text is drawn as outlines by default; plt.rcParams['svg.fonttype'] = 'none' keeps it as editable text, which then needs the same fonts on the computer that opens it.

Make figures from a script, not by hand: fixed random seeds, one function per figure, a loop that saves each into a figures folder with a descriptive name, and plt.close(fig) after every save, because Matplotlib warns once more than 20 figures are open.

"""Capstone: rebuild every figure in the reef report from the CSV files, in one run.

Run it with:  python make_figures.py
Each function returns one figure; save() writes it as PNG (200 dpi) and SVG into figures/.
"""
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

OUT = Path("figures")
BLUE, VERMILLION, GREY = "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#BBBBBB"


def load():
    reef = pd.read_csv("reef_surveys.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
    fish = pd.read_csv("fish_lengths.csv")
    return reef, fish


def save(fig, name):
    """Save one figure as PNG and SVG, then close it to free its memory."""
    OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    fig.savefig(OUT / f"{name}.png", dpi=200)
    fig.savefig(OUT / f"{name}.svg")
    plt.close(fig)
    print("saved", name)


def cover_by_site(reef, fish):
    """An example to replace or improve: mean coral cover by site, sorted, bars starting at zero."""
    cover = reef.groupby("site")["coral_cover_pct"].mean().sort_values()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4), layout="constrained")
    ax.barh(cover.index, cover.values, color=[BLUE if s == cover.index[0] else GREY for s in cover.index])
    ax.set_xlim(0, 60)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.set_title(f"{cover.index[0]} has the lowest mean coral cover", loc="left")
    ax.set_xlabel("Mean coral cover, 2024-2025 (%)")
    return fig


FIGURES = {
    "cover_by_site": cover_by_site,
    # "bleaching_over_time": bleaching_over_time,   # add your own functions here
}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    reef, fish = load()
    for name, make in FIGURES.items():
        save(make(reef, fish), name)
